content: The evidence review aimed to assess the effectiveness of infection prevention and control (IPC) programs. One key component identified was the auditing of IPC practices and providing timely feedback to all relevant staff at the facility level. The primary outcomes evaluated were healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and hand hygiene compliance. Six studies were included in the review: one randomized controlled trial (RCT), two controlled before-and-after studies, one interrupted time series, and two non-controlled before-and-after studies. Five of these studies were conducted in high-income countries, while one was from an upper-middle-income country. Daily audits of adherence to bundle strategies, combined with regular feedback, demonstrated reductions in ventilator-associated pneumonia and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) acquisition. Predefined process indicators for catheter insertion improved with periodic auditing and personalized feedback. Peer assessments with anonymous feedback effectively enhanced universal precaution measures, and the use of a comprehensive checklist covering a wide range of care practices reduced the prevalence of all HAIs. Additionally, internal audits on hand hygiene and catheter-hub care in neonates reduced cases of bacteremia caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) considered the evidence to be of low quality due to medium to high risk of bias across studies and varied study designs. One additional non-controlled before-and-after study supported the use of periodic audits and timely feedback for IPC practices. This study demonstrated that remote video auditing with feedback (using visual cues and electronic reports) significantly increased hand hygiene compliance compared to remote video auditing alone. No studies were found on patient values and preferences regarding this intervention. However, the GDG expressed confidence that patients would value regular evaluation of IPC practices to improve care quality. Healthcare providers, policymakers, and the health workforce are also likely to prioritize routine monitoring and feedback as part of a multifaceted IPC program. The GDG acknowledged that implementing auditing processes requires dedicated time, additional human resources, and specific training for assessors to ensure reliable data collection. This expertise is often limited in low-resource settings, but it is essential to provide such training to achieve accurate evaluations. The GDG emphasized the importance of conducting audits in a non-punitive, blame-free environment to foster improvement and learning. The GDG recommended establishing a national IPC monitoring and evaluation program to assess adherence to standards and the performance of activities aligned with program goals. Hand hygiene monitoring with feedback should be considered a key performance indicator at the national level. The GDG supported the use of the WHO hand hygiene self-assessment tool as a minimum requirement across facilities, with results shared at the national level for benchmarking and at the facility level for local improvement. Despite the focus on hand hygiene, the GDG highlighted the need to explore other critical aspects of IPC, such as catheter-related bloodstream infections, ventilator-associated pneumonia, catheter-associated urinary tract infections, environmental cleaning, and disinfection. Innovative monitoring methods, such as electronic or infrared systems, should also be explored to enhance traditional approaches. The GDG concluded that regular audits and timely feedback of healthcare practices, in line with IPC standards, are essential for preventing HAIs and reducing antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Feedback should be provided to all audited individuals and relevant staff. The GDG also noted a lack of high-quality published evidence on IPC practices beyond hand hygiene and called for further research to address these gaps.
